subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
passage: Salma dropped her bag on the sofa. "Mummy, I have so much homework!" Her mother Manjula sat down beside her. "Tell me what it is." "Sums. Then Hindi writing, one paragraph. Also a drawing." "How long will each take?" Salma looked at the ceiling. "Sums, ten minutes. No, twenty. The paragraph, um, ten. The drawing is thirty." She counted on her fingers. "Twenty and ten and thirty... that is one hour." She blinked. "Only one hour?" "Only one hour," said Manjula. Salma took a pencil and wrote the three tasks on a page.

qa.q: How long did Salma guess the drawing would take?
qa.a: She guessed the drawing would take thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Salma feel when she found the total was one hour?
qa.a: She was surprised and relieved. Her blink and the words "Only one hour?" show the homework stopped seeming so big.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help if Salma still feels worried, and why?
qa.a: She could set a timer for each task and tick it off. Watching the list shrink shows her the work is really finishing.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Salma's list?
qa.a: Manjula sees a daughter who turned a heap of worry into three tasks she can count, and she only had to ask how long each would take.

grounding: A Class 5 child lists her tasks and estimates the minutes, and the one-hour total makes the work feel finite.

subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
passage: Last Monday I came home from school with a mountain of Class 5 homework, or that's how it felt. I flopped on the bed and wanted to cry. Then I remembered something Ma'am once said, and took a page. I wrote: maths sums, Hindi paragraph, drawing of the water cycle. Next to each I guessed a time. Sums, ten minutes; there were only six. Hindi, twenty, because I'm slow at writing. Drawing, thirty, because I like to colour properly. I added them up. One hour. Only one hour! Dhruv, my little brother, peeped in. "Binita didi, will you play?" I said, "After one hour." And I meant it.

qa.q: How much time did Binita guess for the drawing?
qa.a: Thirty minutes, because Binita likes to colour properly.

qa.q: How did Binita feel before and after adding up the times?
qa.a: Binita felt overwhelmed at first, as if the homework were a mountain, then relieved and more confident once the total came to one hour 😊

qa.q: What else could Binita try if her guesses turn out wrong?
qa.a: She could check the clock after each task and adjust her next guess; the list still helps because it breaks the work into clear pieces.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Binita's plan?
qa.a: Dhruv wanted to play straight away, but 'after one hour' gives him a clear time to wait for, which is easier than a vague 'later'.

grounding: Shows a Class 5 child listing three homework tasks, guessing a time for each, and finding the total is one hour, which makes the work feel finite.

subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
passage: Tutor's note, Thursday. Devika arrived in a flap, saying she had "too much" homework and would never finish. I asked her to write it all down instead of worrying about it. She made a list: maths sums, Hindi paragraph, map drawing. Then, without my help, she wrote a guess beside each: 10, 20, 30 minutes. She added them under her breath. "That's one hour. That's not too much." Her shoulders dropped. Nandini, who sits next to her, asked if she could copy the idea for her own homework. Devika finished five minutes over her guess. I'll suggest this to her parents at pickup.

qa.q: How long over her guess did Devika finish?
qa.a: She finished five minutes over her guess.

qa.q: What do Devika's dropping shoulders suggest?
qa.a: She felt relieved and calmer once the total came to one hour, after arriving flustered about 'too much' homework.

qa.q: What might the note-writer suggest if Devika's guesses are often off?
qa.a: Write the real time beside each guess, so her estimates improve; the list already turned a scary pile into a clear hour.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Devika's list?
qa.a: Nandini finds it useful enough to ask to copy the idea for her own homework.

grounding: Illustrates a child listing her homework tasks, estimating ten, twenty and thirty minutes, and seeing the total is only one hour.
